Compute the average derivative effect

Source: R/ade.R
ade.Rd

ade() computes the average derivative effect (ADE) from a shift curve, which is the derivative of the shift curve at a shift of 0.

Usage

ade(x, subset = NULL, outcome = NULL, eps = 1e-05)

Arguments

x

a shift_curve object; the output of a call to shift_curve(), or of reference_curve() or curve_contrast() applied to one.

subset

an optional logical expression indicating the subset of the subgroups for which to compute the ADE. Can only be used when by was supplied to the original call to shift_curve(), and only to refer to variables defining subgroups.

outcome

an optional character vector naming the categories of the outcome for which to compute the ADE. Can only be used when the model gives a separate prediction for each category of the outcome (e.g., multinomial and ordinal models); see the section Categorical outcomes in Details of adrf().

eps

numeric; the step size to use when calculating the numerical derivative, relative to the range of shifts at which the shift curve was computed: the step is eps times a quarter of that range. Default is 1e-5 (.00001).

Value

An object of class ade_est, which is like a curve_est object but with one estimate per subgroup (or per contrast) and no column for the shift. summary(), coef(), and vcov() work as they do for curve_est objects; see summary.curve_est().

Details

With an additive shift, the ADE is \(E[\partial \mu(A, X) / \partial a]\), where \(\mu(a, x)\) is the expected outcome given treatment \(a\) and covariates \(x\): the slope of the outcome with respect to the treatment for each unit at the treatment it actually received, averaged over units. It is the change in the mean outcome per unit of an infinitesimal shift of every unit's treatment (Hines, Diaz-Ordaz, & Vansteelandt, 2026). Because it involves only treatment values near those actually received, it requires positivity only locally, whereas the ADRF and its derivative, the AMEF, require that every unit could have received each treatment value in the range.

The ADE differs from the AMEF averaged over the treatment. The AMEF at a treatment value \(a\) averages the slope at \(a\) over the distribution of the covariates in the whole sample, whereas the ADE averages each unit's slope at its own treatment value. The two coincide when the treatment is unrelated to the covariates (e.g., in a randomized trial) but differ otherwise. A single-number summary of the ADRF itself is the slope of its linear projection; see curve_projection().

With shift_fun = "multiplicative" in shift_curve(), the ADE is \(E[A \, \partial \mu(A, X) / \partial a]\), the change in the mean outcome per unit proportional increase in every unit's treatment; multiplying it by .01 gives the change for a 1% increase. More generally, for a function \(g(a, \delta)\) supplied to shift_fun, the ADE averages each unit's slope weighted by the derivative of \(g\) with respect to \(\delta\) at 0. ade() can only be used when \(g(a, 0) = a\) for every unit, i.e., when a shift of 0 leaves every unit's treatment unchanged, and when the range of shifts in x includes 0.

The ADE is computed as the derivative of the interpolated shift curve at 0, using the same method as amef(), and its standard error is computed from that of the shift curve using the delta method, or from the bootstrap replicates or posterior draws of the shift curve when those are used. For smooth outcome models, it agrees closely with the ADE computed directly from the predictions (e.g., by marginaleffects::avg_slopes()) and does not depend on the range of shifts. For outcome models whose predictions are step functions of the treatment (e.g., Bayesian additive regression trees with hard decision rules), the derivative of each unit's prediction is 0 almost everywhere, and the ADE computed from the shift curve reflects the change in the mean outcome over the spacing of the grid of shifts, which depends on shift and n in the call to shift_curve(); in that case, the effects of specific shifts computed using reference_curve() are easier to interpret than the ADE. Bayesian additive regression trees with soft (smooth) decision rules have predictions that are smooth in the treatment, so the ADE does not depend on the grid.

The default unconditional standard errors account for sampling from the population, which matters when the slope varies across units. The ADE of a contrast between subgroups (i.e., when x is the output of curve_contrast()) is the difference between the ADEs in those subgroups. When x contains shift curves for several subgroups, summary.curve_est() computes simultaneous confidence intervals across the subgroups by default; set simultaneous = FALSE for pointwise intervals.

References

Hines, O. J., Diaz-Ordaz, K., & Vansteelandt, S. (2026). Parameterizing the effect of a continuous treatment using average derivative effects. Biometrika, 113(2), asag012. doi:10.1093/biomet/asag012

See also

  • shift_curve() for estimating a shift curve

  • amef() for computing the derivative of an effect curve

  • summary.curve_est() for performing inference on the ADE

  • curve_projection() for summarizing an ADRF with the slope of its linear projection

  • marginaleffects::avg_slopes() for computing the ADE with conditional inference

Examples

data("nhanes3lead")

fit <- lm(Math ~ poly(logBLL, 5) *
            Male * (Age + Race + PIR +
                      Enough_Food),
          data = nhanes3lead)

# Shift curve of logBLL on Math, unconditional
# inference
sc <- shift_curve(fit, treat = "logBLL")

# ADE of logBLL on Math
ade(sc) |>
  summary()
#>         Average Derivative Effect Estimates
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  Estimate Std. Error       t P-value  CI Low CI High
#>   -0.5335     0.2142 -2.4907  0.0128 -0.9536 -0.1135
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inference: unconditional, pointwise
#> Confidence level: 95% (t* = 1.961, df = 2437)
#> Null value: 0

# ADEs within subgroups and their difference
sc_by <- shift_curve(fit, treat = "logBLL",
                     by = ~Male)

ade(sc_by) |>
  summary()
#>            Average Derivative Effect Estimates
#> ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  Male Estimate Std. Error       t P-value  CI Low CI High
#>     0  -0.5520     0.3553 -1.5539  0.2261 -1.3470  0.2429
#>     1  -0.5157     0.2440 -2.1130  0.0682 -1.0618  0.0305
#> ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inference: unconditional, simultaneous
#> Confidence level: 95% (t* = 2.238, df = 2437)
#> Null value: 0

curve_contrast(sc_by) |>
  ade() |>
  summary()
#>                Average Derivative Effect Contrast Estimates
#> ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>                 Contrast Estimate Std. Error      t P-value  CI Low CI High
#>  [Male = 1] - [Male = 0]   0.0364      0.431 0.0844  0.9327 -0.8088  0.8816
#> ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inference: unconditional, pointwise
#> Confidence level: 95% (t* = 1.961, df = 2437)
#> Null value: 0
